headline: Indiana shoppers count every dollar, then spend the most on what feels local.
summary: Indianapolis is a mid-income, price-aware market where the Pacers share one wallet with the Fever, Purdue, IU and the high school gym. A flat 7% state sales tax and no tax-free weekend mean promotions and bundles do the work tax holidays do elsewhere. Cold, wet Octobers to March make layering and outerwear the real volume story.

insights.title: No tax holiday, so promotions set the calendar
insights.detail: Indiana charges a flat 7% state sales tax on clothing and has no back-to-school tax-free weekend. Shoppers follow retailer promotions, Black Friday and early school starts. Many districts open in late July or the first week of August. Spend also peaks around the Pacers' playoff runs, Black Friday through Christmas, the March high school tournament and early-August back-to-school.
insights.implication: Time kids' and teen drops and footwear promotions to the last two weeks of July, not September. Lead with bundles instead of tax-holiday messaging.

insights.title: One household, many teams
insights.detail: The Pacers, Fever, Colts, Purdue, Indiana and the local high school all compete for the same wallet. Indiana fans routinely wear college and high school gear to NBA games.
insights.implication: Price Pacers product to sit comfortably beside a college hoodie. Build on shared-state motifs, such as the Indiana outline and the gym itself, not just team marks, so product works across fandoms.

insights.title: Fever demand is a second engine
insights.detail: The Indiana Fever's Caitlin Clark era made Indianapolis one of the strongest women's basketball merchandise markets. Its summer sales peak fills the Pacers' off-season.
insights.implication: Plan women's and youth basketball product and a shared Indy basketball story for May to September, so retail runs year-round. Confirm that Fever licensing is separate from the Pacers.

insights.title: Cold-weather layering drives volume
insights.detail: Winters are gray, cold and often snowy, and the shoulder season runs from October into April. Fleeces, hoodies, warm-ups and beanies outsell tees for most of the NBA season.
insights.implication: Lead with warm-ups, quarter-zips, crewnecks and outerwear in Pacers navy, gold and gray. Save shorts and tees for May to August.

insights.title: Team store, big-box and online come first
insights.detail: Fans buy at the arena team store on game night. They also shop malls and big-box stores (Fashion Mall at Keystone, Castleton Square), buy from Fanatics and Nike online, and use resale. Line culture and raffles are thin compared with coastal cities.
insights.implication: Build the plan on arena-night availability and a strong online release. Treat limited drops as an event layered on Moments Mixtape, not the base plan.

insights.title: Jersey buying is generational and value-led
insights.detail: Reggie Miller's number 31 is the heritage jersey for adults. Kids and teens lean to Haliburton. Most purchases are replica or swingman, with plenty of price-led knockoff and resale buying.
insights.implication: Prioritize youth sizes and a clear step-down tier below Swingman. Sell Reggie heritage product as a gift and nostalgia play, and Haliburton as the volume name.

insights.title: Indy is a visitor retail city
insights.detail: Gen Con in the summer, the Indy 500 in May and NCAA and conference events bring out-of-town shoppers downtown and to the arena. So will the Hinkle NBA Cup final on Dec 11.
insights.implication: Stock Indy-only graphics in downtown retail and the team store: Hinkle if cleared, the Indy skyline, generic racing cues and no literal checkered flag. Keep the Cup final in mind for a limited-run tie-in.

watchouts: Butler, Purdue, Indiana and IHSAA marks need separate licensing. Don't blur college and Pacers marks.
Indianapolis Motor Speedway and Indy 500 imagery is licensed. Don't use checkered or 500 marks without clearance.
Keep Fever and Pacers product distinct. Don't assume one fanbase transfers to the other.
Avoid hillbilly or rural stereotypes when using small-town gym imagery. Credit and partner with real communities.

extra.priceProfile: A Midwest market, mid-income and value-oriented, with a wide gap between the affluent north-side suburbs (Carmel, Fishers, Zionsville) and lower-income urban neighborhoods and small towns. A flat 7% state sales tax with no tax holiday keeps shoppers promotion-sensitive. Tier product with a strong entry price, a solid mid-tier and a limited premium layer.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Replicas and Swingman dominate over pro-level versions, and kids' sizes and gifting drive the base. Reggie Miller 31 is the heritage staple and Haliburton the youth and volume name. A noticeable knockoff and resale segment exists. Tees and hoodies outsell jerseys in volume.
